How to understand your lab results
A result must be interpreted with the reference interval printed by the testing laboratory. Laboratories may use different methods and intervals. An out-of-range result does not by itself establish illness; a result inside the interval does not guarantee health. Symptoms, history, medicines and test preparation can affect interpretation.

Liver function tests
A liver panel includes measurements of enzymes, proteins and bilirubin. ALT and AST are enzymes; albumin is a protein made by the liver. These results can provide information about liver injury or function, but a panel alone does not identify the cause of an abnormal result. Interpretation uses the pattern, other tests and clinical information.

Creatinine test
Creatinine is a waste product associated with muscle activity that kidneys remove from blood. Blood or urine creatinine measurements help assess kidney function. Muscle mass, diet and other factors can influence the result. A clinician may combine creatinine with other information, including an estimated filtration rate, rather than interpreting a single value alone.

Cholesterol levels
A lipid panel measures cholesterol and triglycerides. LDL and HDL carry cholesterol in the blood. Interpretation considers cardiovascular risk factors and the full profile, not a single value alone. Fasting requirements depend on the ordered test and laboratory instructions. A calculated result and a directly measured result should not be treated as interchangeable.

Hemoglobin A1c test
HbA1c measures the proportion of hemoglobin with glucose attached and reflects blood glucose exposure over roughly the preceding three months. It differs from a glucose test at a single moment. Certain blood disorders and other conditions can affect its accuracy. A clinician considers these limitations before using the result for diagnosis or monitoring.

Complete blood count
A complete blood count measures blood cells and related indices. Hemoglobin carries oxygen; hematocrit describes the red-cell share of blood volume; MCV describes average red-cell size. White-cell and platelet counts provide different information. Results can be affected by hydration, medicines and other factors, so a pattern requires clinical context and sometimes additional tests.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone test
TSH is produced by the pituitary and helps regulate thyroid hormone production. A TSH result may be assessed alongside thyroid hormones such as T4 and additional tests. TSH alone does not explain why a thyroid problem may be present. Medicines and clinical circumstances can affect how the results are interpreted.

Potassium blood test
Potassium is an electrolyte involved in muscle and nerve function, including heart function. Both high and low blood potassium can be important. Interpretation also considers kidney function and medicines. Sample collection problems can affect the result. A report marked critical should be discussed promptly with the responsible healthcare service rather than managed by a chatbot.

Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio compares urine albumin with urine creatinine to help identify kidney damage. Transient factors can affect albumin in urine, so an abnormal result may require repeat testing and clinical assessment. Preserve the reported unit and ratio; a urine concentration alone is not the same as the ratio.
